questions.question: The taxi fare rises from R20 to R24 and daily riders fall from 1 000 to 950. Calculate the price elasticity of demand, state the sign convention, and classify the demand.
questions.expected_answer: Price change: 4/20 x 100 = 20% increase. Quantity change: 50/1000 x 100 = 5% decrease. Elasticity = 5%/20% = 0,25 (strictly −0,25; the negative sign reflects the inverse price-quantity relationship and we interpret the absolute value). Since 0,25 is less than one, demand is inelastic — riders barely respond to the fare increase.

questions.question: Name and explain three determinants of price elasticity of demand, each with a South African example in a because-sentence.
questions.expected_answer: Any three of: availability of substitutes — one cooldrink brand is elastic because a rival brand sits on the same shelf, while a taxi route with no bus alternative is inelastic; necessity versus luxury — maize meal is inelastic because households must eat, while restaurant meals are elastic because they can be postponed; share of income — matches are inelastic because they claim cents, while rent is elastic(er) because it moves hundreds of rands; time — petrol is inelastic in the week of a price jump but more elastic after a year because buyers form lift clubs or buy smaller cars; habit — cigarettes are inelastic because addiction blocks the escape route, which is why sin taxes raise reliable revenue.

questions.question: Using the chocolate numbers (price R25 to R30, sales 400 to 280), show what happens to total revenue and state the full three-line rulebook linking elasticity and revenue.
questions.expected_answer: Before: R25 x 400 = R10 000. After: R30 x 280 = R8 400 — revenue fell R1 600 because demand is elastic (1,5). Rulebook: with inelastic demand, price and total revenue move in the same direction, so a price rise raises revenue; with elastic demand they move in opposite directions, so a price cut raises revenue; at unitary elasticity small price changes leave revenue unchanged — revenue is at its peak. Caution: revenue is not profit, since extra sales carry extra costs.
